**Yakut** ([/jəˈkuːt/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [_yə- KOOT_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-2) also known as **Sakha** ([/səˈxɑː/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [_sə- KHAH_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) or **Yakutian** , is a [Siberian Turkic language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_Turkic_language "Siberian Turkic language") spoken by around 450,000 native speakers—primarily by ethnic [Yakuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts "Yakuts"), but also by the [Evenki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evenki_people "Evenki people"), [Even](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Even_people "Even people"), [Yukaghir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yukaghir "Yukaghir") and the [Starozhily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starozhily "Starozhily") peoples. It is one of the official languages of the [Sakha Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakha_Republic "Sakha Republic"), a [republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republics_of_Russia "Republics of Russia") in the [Russian Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Federation "Russian Federation").
The Yakut language has a large number of loanwords of [Mongolic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolic_languages "Mongolic languages") origin, a layer of vocabulary of unclear origin, as well as numerous recent borrowings from [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"). Like other Turkic languages, Yakut is an [agglutinative language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agglutinative_language "Agglutinative language") and features [vowel harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowel_harmony "Vowel harmony").
## Classification
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakut_language&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Classification")]
Yakut is a member of the [Northeastern Common Turkic family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_Turkic_languages "Siberian Turkic languages") of languages, which also includes [Shor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shor_language "Shor language"), [Tuvan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_language "Tuvan language") and [Dolgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolgan_language "Dolgan language"). Like most [Turkic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkic_languages "Turkic languages"), Yakut has [vowel harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowel_harmony "Vowel harmony"), is [agglutinative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agglutinative_language "Agglutinative language") and has no [grammatical gender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammatical_gender "Grammatical gender"). Word order is usually [subject–object–verb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subject%E2%80%93object%E2%80%93verb "Subject–object–verb"). Yakut has been influenced by [Tungusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungusic_languages "Tungusic languages") and [Mongolian languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolian_languages "Mongolian languages").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEForsyth1994p.56:_"Their_language...Turkic_in_its_vocabulary_and_grammar,_shows_the_influence_of_both_Tungus_and_Mongolian."-3)
Historically, Yakut left the community of [Common Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Turkic "Common Turkic") speakers relatively early.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJohanson202120,_24-4) Due to this, it diverges in many ways from other Turkic languages and mutual intelligibility between Yakut and other Turkic languages is low[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStachowskiMenz1998-5) and many cognate words are hard to notice when heard. Nevertheless, Yakut contains many features which are important for the reconstruction of [Proto-Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Turkic_language "Proto-Turkic language"), such as the preservation of long vowels.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJohanson202119-6) Even with significant divergent features, Sakha (i.e. Yakut) is typically grouped with the [Common Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Turkic_languages "Common Turkic languages") branch of the family rather than the [Oghuric branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oghuric_languages "Oghuric languages") with [Chuvash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuvash_language "Chuvash language"). A relatively few scholars ([Vasily Radlov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Radlov "Vasily Radlov"), [Otto von Böhtlingk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_von_B%C3%B6htlingk "Otto von Böhtlingk"), and others) have expressed the view that Sakha (i.e. Yakut) is not Turkic.
## Geographic distribution
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakut_language&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geographic distribution")]
Yakut is spoken mainly in the [Sakha Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakha_Republic "Sakha Republic"). It is also used by ethnic Yakuts in [Khabarovsk Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khabarovsk_Region "Khabarovsk Region") and a small diaspora in other parts of the [Russian Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Federation "Russian Federation"), [Kazakhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan "Kazakhstan"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") and other parts of the world. [Dolgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolgan_language "Dolgan language"), a close relative of Yakut, which formerly was considered by some a dialect of Yakut,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAntonov1997-7) is spoken by [Dolgans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolgans "Dolgans") in [Krasnoyarsk Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krasnoyarsk_Region "Krasnoyarsk Region"). Yakut is widely used as a [lingua franca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingua_franca "Lingua franca") by other ethnic minorities in the [Sakha Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakha_Republic "Sakha Republic") – more [Dolgans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolgans "Dolgans"), [Evenks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evenks "Evenks"), [Evens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evens "Evens") and [Yukagirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yukagirs "Yukagirs") speak Yakut rather than their own languages. About 8% of people of ethnicities other than Yakut living in Sakha claimed knowledge of the Yakut language in the [2002 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Russian_Census "2002 Russian Census").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-8)

Yakut is in many ways phonologically unique among the [Turkic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkic_languages "Turkic languages"). Yakut and the closely related [Dolgan language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolgan_language "Dolgan language") are the only Turkic languages without [postalveolar sibilants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibilant#Tongue_shape "Sibilant"). Additionally, no known Turkic languages other than Yakut and [Khorasani Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khorasani_Turkic_language "Khorasani Turkic language") have the palatal nasal /[ɲ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_palatal_nasal "Voiced palatal nasal")/.
#### Consonant assimilation
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakut_language&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Consonant assimilation")]

#### Debuccalization
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakut_language&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Debuccalization")]
Yakut initial **s-** corresponds to initial **h-** in Dolgan and played an important operative rule in the development of proto-Yakut, ultimately resulting in initial **Ø-** < ***h-** < ***s-** (example: Dolgan **h** uoq and Yakut **s** uox, both meaning "not").[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] The historical change of _*s_ > _h_ , known as [debuccalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debuccalization "Debuccalization"), is a common sound-change across the world's languages, being characteristic of such language groups as Greek and Indo-Iranian in their development from Proto-Indo-European, as well as such Turkic languages as Bashkir, e.g. **höt** 'milk' < ***süt**.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-18)
Debuccalization is also an active phonological process in modern Yakut. Intervocalically the phoneme /[s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_alveolar_fricative "Voiceless alveolar fricative")/ becomes [[h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_glottal_fricative "Voiceless glottal fricative")]. #### Vowel harmony
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakut_language&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Vowel harmony")]
Like other [Turkic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowel_harmony#Turkic_languages "Vowel harmony"), a characteristic feature of Yakut is [progressive vowel harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowel_harmony "Vowel harmony"). Most root words obey vowel harmony, for example in **кэлин** (_kelin_) 'back', all the vowels are front and unrounded, whereas in **олоборун** (_oloborun_) 'I live', all the vowels are back and rounded. Yakut's vowel harmony in suffixes is the most complex system in the Turkic family.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJohanson2021315-30) Vowel harmony is an [assimilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assimilation_\(linguistics\) "Assimilation \(linguistics\)") process where vowels in one syllable take on certain features of vowels in the preceding syllable. In Yakut, subsequent vowels all take on [frontness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowel#Acoustics "Vowel") and all non-low vowels take on [lip rounding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lip_rounding "Lip rounding") of preceding syllables' vowels.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrueger196248%E2%80%939StachowskiMenz1998419-31) There are two main rules of vowel harmony:
  1. Frontness/backness harmony: 
    1. Front vowels are always followed by front vowels.
    2. Back vowels are always followed by back vowels.
  2. Rounding harmony: 
    1. Unrounded vowels are always followed by unrounded vowels.
    2. Close rounded vowels always occur after close rounded vowels.
    3. Open unrounded vowels **do not** assimilate in rounding with close rounded vowels.


The quality of the diphthongs /ie, ïa, uo, üö/ for the purposes of vowel harmony is determined by the first segment in the diphthong. Taken together, these rules mean that the pattern of subsequent syllables in Yakut is entirely predictable, and all words will follow the following pattern:[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJohanson2021316-32) Like the [consonant assimilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#Consonant_assimilation) rules above, suffixes display numerous allomorphs determined by the stem they attach to. There are two [archiphoneme vowels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoneme#Neutralization_and_archiphonemes "Phoneme") _I_ (an underlyingly high vowel) and _A_ (an underlyingly low vowel).

## Grammar
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakut_language&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Grammar")]
### Syntax
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakut_language&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Syntax")]
The typical word order can be summarized as [subject](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subject_\(grammar\) "Subject \(grammar\)") – [adverb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adverb "Adverb") – [object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_\(grammar\) "Object \(grammar\)") – [verb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verb "Verb"); [possessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Possession_\(linguistics\) "Possession \(linguistics\)") – [possessed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Possession_\(linguistics\) "Possession \(linguistics\)"); [adjective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjective "Adjective") – [noun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noun "Noun").

### Grammatical number
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakut_language&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Grammatical number")]
Nouns have plural and singular forms. The plural is formed with the suffix /-LAr/, which may surface as **-лар** (_-lar_), **-лэр** (_-ler_), **-лөр** (_-lör_), **-лор** (_-lor_), **-тар** (_-tar_), **-тэр** (_-ter_), **-төр** (_-tör_), **-тор** (_-tor_), **-дар** (_-dar_), **-дэр** (_-der_), **-дөр** (_-dör_), **-дор** (_-dor_), **-нар** (_-nar_), **-нэр** (_-ner_), **-нөр** (_-nör_), or **-нор** (_-nor_), depending on the preceding consonants and vowels. The plural is used only when referring to a number of things collectively, not when specifying an amount. Nouns have no [gender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammatical_gender "Grammatical gender").

### Nominal inflection (cases)
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakut_language&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Nominal inflection \(cases\)")]
Only Sakha (Yakut) has a rich case system that differs markedly from all the other [Siberian Turkic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_Turkic_languages "Siberian Turkic languages"). It has retained the ancient comitative case from [Old Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Turkic "Old Turkic") (due to strong influence from [Mongolian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolian_language "Mongolian language")) while in other [Turkic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkic_languages "Turkic languages"), the old comitative has become an instrumental case. However, in Sakha language the Old Turkic locative case has come to denote partitive case, thus leaving no case form for the function of locative. Instead, locative, dative and allative cases are realized through Common Turkic dative suffix:

The Yakut lexicon includes loans from Russian, Mongolic, Evenki, and number of words from other languages or of unknown origin. The Mongolic loans do not appear to be traceable to any specific Mongolic language, but a few have been traced to [Buryat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buryat_language "Buryat language") and [Khalkha Mongolian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalkha_Mongolian "Khalkha Mongolian"). They are widely dispersed through various categories of words with words relating to the home and law having the most Mongolic loans. Russian loans on the contrary are much more widespread but less evenly dispersed though various types of words. Words relating to the modern world, clothing, and the home have the most Russian influence.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-59)
## Oral and written literature
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakut_language&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Oral and written literature")]
The Yakut have a tradition of oral epic in their language called Олоҥхо ("[Olonkho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olonkho "Olonkho")"), traditionally performed by skilled performers. The subject matter is based on Yakut mythology and legends. Versions of many Olonkho poems have been written down and translated since the 19th century, but only a very few older performers of the oral Olonkho tradition are still alive. They have begun a program to teach young people to sing this in their language and revive it, though in a modified form.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-60)
The first printing in Yakut was a part of a book by [Nicolaas Witsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaas_Witsen "Nicolaas Witsen") published in 1692 in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-61)
In 2005, Marianne Beerle-Moor, director of the [Institute for Bible Translation, Russia/CIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_Bible_Translation "Institute for Bible Translation"), was awarded the Order of Civil Valour by the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia) for the translation of the [New Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Testament "New Testament") into Yakut.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-62)
Probably the first-ever Islamic book in Sakha language, "Билсиҥ: Ислам" ("Get to know: Islam"), written by a Sakha convert born in the village of [Asyma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asyma "Asyma"), was published in 2012.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language#cite_note-63) This short book (52 pages) is intended to be a condensed introduction to the fundamentals of Islam in Sakha. The author occasionally employs native terms (which are also used in [Olonkho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olonkho "Olonkho") corpus) to render some Islamic concepts, such as the [jinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinn "Jinn").
